cls: Amide local anesthetic / class Ib antiarrhythmic
quick: Infiltration/nerve block: max 4.5 mg/kg (300 mg) plain; 7 mg/kg (500 mg) with epinephrine
Category B; use only if clearly needed
Excretion in milk unknown; use with caution

Not directly relevant; CNS effects additive
ECG, blood pressure, CNS status, signs of toxicity
summary: Lidocaine is an amide-type local anesthetic used to produce local or regional anesthesia by infiltration, peripheral nerve block, and epidural/caudal techniques; it is also used intravenously as a class Ib antiarrhythmic for ventricular arrhythmias. It is contraindicated in patients hypersensitive to amide local anesthetics. Systemic toxicity from excessive dose or inadvertent intravascular injection produces CNS excitation/depression and cardiovascular collapse.
indications: Production of local or regional anesthesia by infiltration techniques
Peripheral nerve block (e.g., brachial plexus, intercostal)
Central neural block (lumbar and caudal epidural)
Intravenous treatment of ventricular arrhythmias (antiarrhythmic use)

dosage.d: Maximum 4.5 mg/kg, not to exceed 300 mg per procedure
dosage.n: Doses are a guide; adjust for site, depth, and patient condition

dosage.d: Maximum 7 mg/kg, not to exceed 500 mg per procedure
dosage.n: Epinephrine prolongs effect and limits systemic absorption

dosage.d: Do not exceed 4.5 mg/kg (or per weight-based limits)
dosage.n: Use the lowest dosage that produces effective anesthesia

dosage.d: Loading 1-1.5 mg/kg IV bolus, then 1-4 mg/min infusion
dosage.n: Reduce in hepatic impairment, heart failure, or shock; monitor levels/ECG

admin: Use the lowest dosage and concentration that produces the desired effect
Aspirate before and during injection to avoid intravascular administration
Use solutions containing epinephrine only when larger volumes are required and vasopressors are not contraindicated
Have resuscitation equipment, oxygen, and lipid emulsion readily available before administration
moa: Lidocaine stabilizes the neuronal membrane by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels, inhibiting the ionic fluxes required for the initiation and conduction of nerve impulses, producing local anesthesia. The same sodium-channel blockade in cardiac tissue underlies its class Ib antiarrhythmic action on ventricular myocardium.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to amide-type local anesthetics
relative: Heart block or severe bradycardia (for antiarrhythmic use without pacing)
Application/injection at infected or inflamed sites

preg: Pregnancy Category B. Animal reproduction studies revealed no fetal harm, but there are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Use only when clearly needed, particularly during early pregnancy; obstetric use can affect the fetus/neonate (bradycardia, CNS depression).
lact: It is not known whether lidocaine is excreted in human milk in clinically significant amounts. Exercise caution when administering to a nursing woman.
renal: Use with caution in severe renal impairment because metabolites (e.g., glycinexylidide) may accumulate, particularly with prolonged infusions; reduce dose accordingly.
hepatic: Lidocaine is metabolized by the liver; in hepatic impairment, heart failure, or reduced hepatic blood flow, clearance falls and the dose (especially infusion rates) should be reduced to avoid accumulation and toxicity.

major: Other antiarrhythmics and class I agents (additive cardiac depression)
Drugs causing methemoglobinemia (nitrates, other local anesthetics, antineoplastics) - additive risk
moderate: Beta-blockers and cimetidine (reduce hepatic clearance, raise lidocaine levels)
MAO inhibitors / tricyclics with epinephrine-containing solutions (severe hypertension)
Phenothiazines and butyrophenones (reduce/reverse epinephrine pressor effect)
minor: Ergot-type oxytocics with vasopressors (severe persistent hypertension)
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; avoid additive CNS depression
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor ECG; methemoglobin level if cyanosis appears unresponsive to oxygen

common: Numbness or tingling around the mouth
rare: High spinal / total spinal block (with neuraxial use)
Persistent neurologic deficit / cauda equina syndrome
Chondrolysis (with intra-articular infusion - not an approved use)

monitoring: Continuous ECG and cardiac rhythm (especially IV/antiarrhythmic use)
State of consciousness and early signs of CNS toxicity after each injection
Oxygen saturation and signs of methemoglobinemia
Plasma lidocaine levels during prolonged infusions where available
counsel: The area will be numb and weak for some hours - protect it from injury, heat, and biting
Report lightheadedness, ringing in the ears, numbness around the mouth, or a metallic taste during injection
Tell the clinician about any prior reaction to local anesthetics
Seek immediate care for difficulty breathing, blue discoloration, palpitations, or seizures
pk: Rapid - local anesthesia within minutes of injection
Depends on site and dose; rapid systemic peak if intravascular
Local anesthesia ~0.5-1 hour (plain), prolonged with epinephrine
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light
pearls: Maximum doses: ~4.5 mg/kg (300 mg) plain; ~7 mg/kg (500 mg) with epinephrine - calculate per patient
Always aspirate before injecting to avoid inadvertent intravascular administration
Lipid emulsion (Intralipid) is the rescue treatment for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)
Reduce dose in hepatic impairment, heart failure, and shock due to reduced clearance
missed: Not applicable - lidocaine is given by a clinician as single procedural doses or a monitored infusion, not by a patient self-dosing schedule.
overdose: Systemic toxicity (from excessive dose, rapid absorption, or intravascular injection) causes progressive CNS excitation (perioral numbness, tinnitus, agitation, twitching, convulsions) followed by CNS depression, then cardiovascular depression (hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmia, arrest). Management: stop injection, secure airway, give 100% oxygen and ventilatory support, control seizures (benzodiazepines), and support circulation; intravenous lipid emulsion (e.g., 20% Intralipid) is the specific rescue for local anesthetic systemic toxicity. Methemoglobinemia is treated with methylene blue.
